subject: Business
title: The Federal Reserve and Interest Rates
description: One-minute skill: The Federal Reserve and Interest Rates.

hook.text: One committee of 12 people in Washington sets the price of money for the entire US economy.

buildup.text: The Federal Reserve controls the federal funds rate — the base rate at which banks lend to each other overnight.

discovery.text: This rate ripples through everything: mortgages, car loans, credit cards, business borrowing, and savings yields.

twist.text: Raising rates slows spending and fights inflation. Lowering rates stimulates borrowing and spending.

climax.text: In 2022, the Fed raised rates from 0% to 5.25% in 18 months — the fastest increase in 40 years — to fight inflation.

punchline.text: When the Fed moves, every wallet in America feels it.

quiz.question: What happens when the Federal Reserve raises interest rates?
options: Borrowing becomes more expensive, which slows spending and fights inflation
Prices immediately drop across all sectors

details.summary: The Federal Reserve controls the federal funds rate, which ripples through the entire economy affecting mortgage rates, savings yields, stock prices, and consumer borrowing costs. Understanding Fed decisions helps you anticipate changes in your financial landscape.
details.whyItMatters: Fed rate decisions directly affect your mortgage payment, savings account yield, and investment returns. Knowing why rates rise or fall helps you time major financial decisions like home purchases or refinancing.
takeaways: The Fed raises rates to cool inflation and lowers them to stimulate growth
Rate changes ripple through mortgages, loans, savings, and stock prices
The federal funds rate is the benchmark that influences all other rates

faq.question: How does the Federal Reserve raising interest rates affect consumers?
faq.answer: Higher rates increase mortgage payments, auto loan costs, and credit card interest charges. Savings accounts and CDs offer better yields. Stock prices often decline initially as borrowing costs rise and future earnings are discounted more heavily.

faq.question: Why does the Fed lower interest rates during recessions?
faq.answer: Lower rates make borrowing cheaper, encouraging consumers to buy homes and cars and businesses to invest and hire. Cheaper credit stimulates spending and economic activity. The risk is that excessively low rates for too long can fuel asset bubbles and inflation.
